title: Back stitch
subtitle: The outline stitch that produces a solid, continuous line.
excerpt: Back stitch produces a solid unbroken line on the surface of the cloth. Each stitch fills the gap left by the previous one, working backward from the end of the last stitch. It is the standard outline stitch for all needlework disciplines.
sourceNotes:
Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopaedia of Needlework (1886), Project Gutenberg #20776. Back stitch technique and applications.
Caulfeild and Saward, Dictionary of Needlework (1882), Internet Archive. Back stitch entry.

glossaryTerms.definition: An outline stitch worked by inserting the needle backward into the end of the last stitch, then bringing it forward two stitch lengths ahead. Produces a solid continuous line on the surface.

content.text: is worked by going backward with the needle each time: the needle comes up two stitch lengths ahead, then goes back into the end of the last stitch. The result is a solid unbroken line on the front of the cloth, with the stitches overlapping on the back.
Anchor the thread and bring the needle up at the start point.
Push the needle back down one stitch length behind the start point.
Bring the needle up two stitch lengths ahead of the start point.
Push the needle back down into the end of the previous stitch (one stitch length back). This is the 'back' in back stitch.
Continue bringing the needle up one stitch length ahead and going back down into the end of the previous stitch.

items.symptom: The line looks broken with small gaps
items.cause: The needle didn't go exactly into the end of the previous stitch, leaving a tiny gap.
items.fix: Before pushing the needle back down, check that it is entering exactly at the end of the last stitch, not next to it.

items.cause: The stitch length varied between stitches.
items.fix: Count threads on evenweave or Aida. On plain fabric, draw a light guideline with a water-soluble pen.

content.text: Back stitch is used for outlines on cross-stitch pieces and as the foundation for blackwork patterns.
is also used in Hardanger and can be worked in a single strand for fine linear detail in surface embroidery.
